case.case_title: Lerins Peiris v. Neil Rupasinghe, Member of Parliament and Others
case.source_citation: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, SC Application 126/99 (FR), decided on 19 November 1999

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the petitioner’s right to freedom of peaceful assembly under Article 14(1)(b) was infringed when he was forcibly excluded from a workshop and assaulted.
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioner claimed that the respondents’ actions prevented him from peacefully assembling and participating in the workshop, violating his constitutional right.
case_context.respondent_argument: Respondents argued that the petitioner left voluntarily after persuasion by police and venue manager and denied responsibility for any violation of assembly rights.
key_facts: The petitioner was invited to a workshop concerning the Muturajawela/Negombo Lagoon System.
Respondents told the petitioner he should be kept out of the meeting and assaulted him.
The petitioner was forced to leave and could not participate in the assembly.
The respondents were acting in their official capacity as elected representatives.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The court recognized freedom of peaceful assembly as a fundamental right essential for democratic participation and expression of public views.
reasoning.application_to_facts: By assaulting the petitioner and forcing him to leave, the respondents effectively prevented him from peacefully assembling and participating in the workshop, violating Article 14(1)(b).
principles_established: Freedom of peaceful assembly is protected against executive action that forcibly excludes participants.
Elected representatives must respect constitutional rights even in public policy forums.
precedents_cited: Wijeratne v. Vijitha Perera and Others
Faiz v. Attorney General and Others
Deshapriya and Another v. Municipal Council, Nuwara Eliya and two others
Channa Pieris v. Attorney General and Others

outcome.holding: The court held that the respondents violated the petitioner’s fundamental right to freedom of peaceful assembly under Article 14(1)(b).
outcome.remedy_or_orders: The respondents were ordered to pay compensation and costs as stated in the judgment.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 14(1)(b) was materially engaged because the petitioner was prevented from peacefully assembling at the workshop, a key fact in the court’s finding of constitutional violation.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: The petitioner was forcibly excluded from the workshop and assaulted, preventing his participation in the assembly; the court found this violated Article 14(1)(b).
